title: Energetics of vertical kilometer foot races; is steeper cheaper?
authors: Giovanelli N, Ortiz ALR, Henninger K, Kram R
population: 15 runners (10 male, 5 female, 32.9 +/- 7.5 yr) walking and running 5 min at 7 angles (9.4 to 39.2 degrees) at a fixed vertical velocity of 0.35 m/s
findings: At every angle other than 9.4 degrees, the vertical cost of walking was lower than that of running (average -8.45 +/- 1.05%, P < 0.001).
Broad minima of vertical cost existed for both gaits between 20.4 and 35.0 degrees (average walking 44.17 +/- 0.41 J/kg/m; running 48.46 +/- 0.35 J/kg/m).
In walking, stride frequency was about 28% slower (and stride length longer) than in running.
The authors conclude that on inclines steeper than 15.8 degrees athletes can reduce energy expenditure by walking rather than running at the vertical velocity tested.
limitations: 15 runners, 5 min treadmill bouts, one vertical velocity (0.35 m/s = 1,260 m/h, derived); no fatigue or technical terrain. The angle at which running stops being cheaper depends on vertical speed.
implications: At a climbing rate of 1,260 m/h, switch to walking above about 15.8 degrees (about 28% grade, derived by tan) because walking was cheaper; at 9.4 degrees (about 17%) it was not.
Treat the walk/run switch as a function of both grade and climbing rate: at 800 m/h another study found the switch at about 7.2 degrees.
Energy per vertical metre has a broad minimum on very steep slopes (20.4-35.0 degrees, about 37-70% grade), so steeper is not more expensive per vertical metre in that range.

verification.notes: Added. Crossref: J Appl Physiol 120(3):370-375, 2016-02-01, four authors match. PubMed PMID 26607247 abstract supports all numbers; degree-to-grade conversions are derived.
